narrative.what_i_did:
The operator opened with two bug reports from field-testing: no way to sign a family they had started, and the People tree still showing them as an org node even after they deleted their org. They asked me to find where the last session had left off and fix from there. I read the prior session.json first per the standing order — the previous carpenter shipped the family-mode substrate plus the StartFamilyModal founder UI plus PeopleTree v1 plus the IdentityChip rollout, and explicitly named the member-side ratify surface and the founder-to-member delivery leg as next-up cuts. That tracked one of the bugs but not the other, so I grounded against the actual code before assuming.

I ran the four gates green up front (typecheck silent, lint silent, 318 of 318 tests in 12.88 seconds, build clean) so the starting state was honestly known, then read StartFamilyModal, FamilyIdentitySections, peopleTreeLayout, OrgDeclarationSection, MembershipChainSheet, createMembership, openMemberRoster, officialsRoster, and inboxEnvelopeHandler. The family bug confirmed: the founder card was render-only with no path to push the envelope anywhere. The org-tree bug took longer to trace — PeopleTree's extractOrgs walks holdings for credential_type='membership' envelopes where the member is the operator, which means the org-self-declaration alone is not what feeds it. The actual feeders are officials rosters (subject=org), open-member rosters (subject=org with org_id leaf), memberships the operator issued to themselves while testing (org_id=me, member_id=me), and self-memberships the operator received as the org (org_id=me). All four carry the operator's identity in their org_id leaf when the operator is the org. The Delete-this-organization affordance only dropped the self-declaration; every other artifact survived. After deletion, extractOrgs still found memberships with member_id matching the operator and produced an org node on the outer ring of the People tree.

Before cutting I asked the operator three chip-form questions per PFOR-019 to pin scope: which family-sign gap, where the org-ness was lingering, and what specifically they had deleted. They answered founder-side send (not member-side ratify, not the whole loop), People-tree-still-has-org-node (not the Identity-tab header card), and Settings delete (not Leave-via-MembershipChainSheet). That made both fixes concrete and bounded.

The org-delete cascade landed in src/features/settings/OrgDeclarationSection.tsx. The new deleteOrgDeclaration collects every envelope id in holdings whose org_id leaf equals wallet.identity, adds the org-self-declaration's id to the set, calls wallet.unhold on each in a loop, then does one save+refresh for the whole batch. The cascade is precisely-scoped: it only matches artifacts that carry the operator's identity as org_id, so memberships the operator holds from OTHER orgs (where org_id is some other pubkey) stay untouched, family-units stay untouched (founder_id not org_id), and handshakes stay untouched (no org_id leaf). The unholdEnvelope prop is no longer used here so I removed it from the component's Props interface, the destructured param, and the SettingsScreen prop pass-through; SettingsScreen's useWallet destructure also drops unholdEnvelope. MembershipChainSheet still uses unholdEnvelope from useWallet for the Leave-organization affordance, so the context surface stays untouched.

The family send-affordance landed in src/features/wallet-core/FamilyIdentitySections.tsx. The component went from pure render to a smart component that pulls wallet + sendEnvelope via useWallet. For each family card it computes whether the operator is the founder (founder_id === wallet.identity), the set of signers so far, and the list of named members other than the founder that have not yet signed. When the operator is the founder and at least one member is unsigned, a 'Send to N unsigned member(s)' button renders below the member list. Tapping it iterates the unsigned non-founder members, calls sendEnvelope(member.pubkey, attestation) for each, summarizes the publish result via summarizePublish, and surfaces a per-card status line in emerald, amber, or red depending on whether all sent, some failed, or all failed. The handler is fire-and-track — it does not block the UI past the in-flight Sending state, and individual sends are awaited sequentially so a flaky relay does not let later sends race ahead of earlier ones in the operator's mental model. The member row inline label gains a '· signed' suffix when that member's pubkey appears in the envelope's signatures list so the operator sees signature progress per-member instead of just the aggregate N-of-M chip.

The inbox silent-absorb path in inboxEnvelopeHandler.ts (the previous cut's substrate I did not have to touch) closes the return leg automatically. When a member ratifies and sends the cosigned envelope back, the founder's wallet recognizes the envelopeId as one it already holds, mergeSignatures detects new signatures, and the merged envelope replaces the held copy. The 'N of M signed' chip on the family card climbs as ratifications arrive without any further code from this cut. The member-side ratify modal — the UI that lets a named member actually sign — is still the next-up cut, which the operator's chip-form answer explicitly deferred.

All four gates green after the changes: typecheck silent, lint silent, 318 of 318 tests in 11.72 seconds, build clean with bundle budgets OK. The wallet-core manifest gained FamilyIdentitySections.tsx in its touches list (a pre-existing gap from the StartFamilyModal cut that I filled while I was here). One commit landed — 29b3c9e — and pushed to the dispatch branch claude/multisig-orgs-status-jiLwm.
narrative.whats_pending:
The family-mode arc has one clear next-up cut: the member-side ratify surface. When a named member's wallet receives a family-unit envelope via Mycelium, the inbox currently surfaces it as a generic 'unknown envelope' row because routeFor does not recognize the family_unit credential_type yet. The cut would add envelope routing for family-unit envelopes plus a FamilyRatifyModal that lets the named member review the family, see who else is in it, and add their signature with one tap. The cosigned envelope then ships back to the founder via Mycelium and the existing silent-absorb path absorbs the new signature into the founder's holdings. This closes the loop end-to-end with no other substrate work.

The tree-v2 family-rendering cut also still waits — branching a family-unit node into its members under the operator's center node in PeopleTree. The substrate is already there (findFamilyUnitsForMember + readFamilyUnit), only the layout-and-rendering layer is missing. Plus the add-birthday-now sibling cut the operator named directly: the operator's own missing birthday because they were the first identity ever signed in their wallet long before the birthday leaf was a thing. Same supplement-credential pattern the family-unit substrate established (credential signed today carrying a backdated as_of leaf for the actual date) solves it.

The five named open future cuts on the PeopleTree v1 maturation remain open: angular sector grouping by category (family cluster on one side rather than scattering by hash), zoom + collapse for trees that grow past one screen, multi-hop expansion (tap a peer, see their friends-of-friends), org-chain walking on org nodes via walkOrgChain, and tap-a-node-for-detail (peer tap opens chat thread, org tap opens membership detail). The four substrate-side candidates from earlier sessions also remain: receiveSelfMembership orgSelfDecl-lookup centralization, JoinOrgModal proof-candidate finder extraction, Phase D charter-amendment chain, and the appcommander metadata cleanup chip.

Field-testing the org-delete cascade and the family-send button on the operator's actual phone is worthwhile before pulling the next thread. The cascade behavior — that deleting an org also drops every officials roster, open-member roster, issued membership, and received self-membership that carried this wallet as org_id — is a meaningful semantic change worth confirming behaves as the operator expects. The family-send button is also the first close-up look at the cross-wallet ratify flow; if the send latency, the per-card status copy, or the post-send signature-count timing feel wrong in the hand, those become input to the next polish pass.
narrative.what_you_could_do_better:
One honest observation. The org-delete cascade matches envelopes purely by their org_id leaf equaling the operator's identity. If a future envelope type adds an org_id leaf for some other reason (an unrelated credential that happens to use that leaf name with the operator's pubkey as its value), the cascade would drop it too. Today no such envelope shape exists, so the cascade is correct for the actual codebase, but the matcher is structurally permissive rather than strict. A stricter version would gate on credential_type as well — only dropping envelopes whose credential_type is one of the four known org-related types (officials, open_member_roster, membership, self_membership). I did not narrow it because the broader match is simpler and the harm of false-positives is bounded (the operator can rebuild any envelope from peers who also hold it, and they explicitly clicked Delete on their org). Naming the seam so a future carpenter who adds a new org_id-carrying envelope type considers whether it should be cascade-deletable.

A second honest note. The family-send handler awaits each sendEnvelope call sequentially. For a family with five named members this is five round-trips to the Mycelium relay back to back. Parallel sends with Promise.all would be faster but harder to surface partial-failure status cleanly, and the sequential pattern matches what the OfficialsEditorModal cosign-request path already does. The latency is acceptable for the family sizes the operator is likely to use today; if family sizes ever grow into the dozens, parallelism would be the natural next polish.

Third, the family-send button does not deduplicate against in-flight sends — if the operator taps it twice quickly, the second tap is blocked by the sendBusy gate, but only after the first tap's setStatusByIndex has run. A fast double-tap could in theory race the state update. In practice the React event loop serializes both within a single render cycle so this is not a real bug, but a useRef-based in-flight guard would be belt-and-suspenders.

Nothing else surfaced beyond the declared scope this session. The two fixes were exactly what the operator's chip-form answers scoped them to be; the gates went green on the first run after the changes; no bundle-budget bumps were required.
narrative.bigger_picture:
The bigger-picture teaching in this cut is what 'delete is a verb that operates on dependencies, not just identities' means at the data substrate. Before this fix, Delete-this-organization removed the claim 'this wallet is an org' but left every artifact the wallet had produced AS that org sitting in holdings — the rosters, the issued memberships, the received self-memberships. Each of those carries the org's identity as org_id leaf, and downstream consumers (PeopleTree's extractOrgs, the membership chain walker, future verifiers) read that leaf as authoritative 'this came from THAT org.' Removing the self-declaration without removing the dependent artifacts is incoherent at the data layer even when it looks clean at the surface. The cascade-delete pattern is the structural fix: dropping the root claim drops everything in the wallet that depended on the root claim being true.

The family-send affordance teaches a different lesson about the friendly-rendering thesis. The operator's diagnosis — 'no way to sign the family I started' — is, at the substrate level, perfectly accurate: the envelope had only the founder's signature and the wallet held no path to add more. But the user did not say 'no path to deliver the envelope to the other named members so they can ratify.' They said 'no way to sign.' That linguistic shorthand is exactly what Layer 4 is supposed to flatten: cryptographically, signing is a per-wallet act that each member's wallet performs on its own; experientially, the operator should be able to think of it as 'I started a family, now I push it through and it gets signed.' The Send-to-members button does not change the cryptography one bit — each member's wallet still produces their own signature with their own private key, still rides their own cosignature back through Mycelium to be absorbed. What changes is that the operator no longer has to mentally model the per-wallet signing act; they just initiate. The substrate is unchanged; the surface flattens.

The broader thesis-level connection is the same Layer 4 framing the previous IdentityChip cut taught: a sovereign-identity wallet succeeds when the cryptographic substrate is invisible to anyone who is not already curious about it. The operator who wants to know what is actually happening on the wire can still see envelope codes, signature counts, ratification badges, and the canonical envelope JSON in the collapse-by-default textareas. The operator who just wants to declare their family and have the people in it ratify it can tap one button, see a status line in plain English, and watch the signed count climb. Both audiences are served by the same code path because the cryptography is the substrate and the UI is the surface — never the other way around. The prime directive applies cleanly: clarity beats cleverness, useful beats flashy, safe beats fast. Cascade-delete makes Delete an honest verb. Send-to-members makes Start-a-family an honest verb. Each makes one operator-facing word match what the substrate actually does under the hood.

feedback_to_appcommander: Three patterns from this cut worth noting for the skeleton. First, the cascade-delete pattern for compound identity claims — when a root claim (this wallet is an org) is removed, every artifact in the wallet that depended on that root claim being true should also be removed in the same atomic operation. The operator-facing 'Delete' verb is incoherent otherwise; the surface says deleted but the substrate is still littered with dependent envelopes that downstream consumers read as authoritative. Worth lifting into the skeleton's CLAUDE.md as a doctrine note: when shipping a delete affordance for a compound claim, the cascade is part of the feature, not a follow-up. Second, the founder-initiates-and-substrate-absorbs pattern the family-send button uses — the operator taps one button, the founder's wallet ships the envelope to each member, each member's wallet ratifies independently via the existing cosign + Mycelium routing, and the silent-absorb path on the founder's wallet merges signatures as they arrive. The operator's mental model is 'I started a family, members signed it' rather than 'I produced an envelope, transmitted it via N parallel channels, each receiver constructed a cosignature, each transmitted back, and the merge engine reconciled the signature sets.' Both descriptions are accurate; only one is field-testable by a non-cryptographer. Third, the chip-form-questions-before-cutting pattern works particularly well for bug-fix sessions where the operator's symptom description is ambiguous about which surface or which underlying envelope is involved. The three chip questions this session asked turned an ambiguous bug report into two concrete fix shapes in under a minute. The PFOR-019 chip-form doctrine is paying off in practice.
